text: New York's subway runs on two steel rails. Let's take the track apart.
The running rails: about a hundred fifteen pounds of steel per yard, four feet eight and a half inches apart.
Tie plates fix them to wooden ties or concrete blocks, on ballast or concrete.
Beside them, the third rail: six hundred twenty-five volts DC, under a cover board.
A contact shoe on the truck slides along it, to power the traction motors.
The wheels aren't flat. Each tread is a slight cone, with a flange on the inside.
In a curve, the outer wheel rides its wider part and covers more ground. The train steers itself.
All that weight sits on contact patches about the size of a dime.
The wheels also short the two rails. That track circuit tells the signals a train is there.
That's why roof riding kills. Tunnel ceilings sit inches above the car. Curves and braking throw you. Below: six hundred twenty-five volts.
Six people died subway surfing in twenty twenty-four. At least five in twenty twenty-five. Subway surfing kills. Don't.
What should we take apart next?
Congrats! You've discovered how a subway train rides its rails.
